editorNote: The personal computer is leaving the lab. This week, Clarkson freshmen collect desktops as routinely as orientation papers, while families face a crowded and fast-changing home-computer aisle.
morningLine: Campus computers, arcade animation, and a sub-$1,000 price war define the week.

lead.headline: A Desktop for Every Freshman
lead.dek: More than 800 new Clarkson students are to collect personal computers during orientation, turning a bold campus requirement into everyday academic equipment.
body: POTSDAM, N.Y. — More than 800 Clarkson College freshmen arriving Thursday will receive an unusual addition to the standard orientation packet: their own personal desktop computers. United Press International reported the distribution on August 24, as the college prepared to put a machine directly into the hands of every member of the incoming class.

Clarkson announced the program the previous October and described itself as the first college in the nation to require every incoming freshman to have a personal computer. The distinction is larger than a crowded computer laboratory. Each student is expected to possess a machine as a regular academic tool, available for assignments, calculation, writing, and experimentation.

The undertaking marks a decisive change in the place of personal computing on campus. Only a few years ago, many undergraduates encountered computers through terminals scheduled around a central system. Clarkson's plan treats the desktop machine more like a textbook: individual, immediate, and woven into daily coursework.

Questions of training, software, maintenance, and how professors will redesign assignments now move to the foreground. Yet the scale of the handout is itself the news. For this class, computer literacy will not be an elective pursuit on the edge of college life; it begins at orientation.

stories.headline: Christmas Computer War Crowds the Aisles
stories.dek: At least 17 machines debuted at summer CES, and COMPUT! expects 30 to 40 sub-$1,000 choices by Christmas.
body: The home-computer counter is becoming a battlefield. COMPUT!'s August survey counted at least 17 personal computers introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show and forecast 30 to 40 machines priced below $1,000 by Christmas.

The range runs from minimal low-memory machines near $40 to elaborate systems above $1,000 with modems, speech, and disk drives. Coleco's Adam is the boldest all-in-one wager: an 80K Z80A computer, high-speed cassette storage, keyboard, daisy-wheel printer, word processing, Microsoft BASIC, and Buck Rogers promised for under $600.

Price alone will not settle the contest. Buyers must judge software, storage, compatibility, dealer support, and whether announced machines actually reach shops. The crowded field gives families leverage but makes every purchase a bet on which platform will survive.

stories.headline: Dragon's Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon
stories.dek: Don Bluth animation and laserdisc playback give players a startling glimpse of a movie-like arcade future.
body: Arcade crowds are gathering around a cabinet that looks unlike the familiar fields of sprites and maze walls. Dragon's Lair uses laserdisc video to display lavish Don Bluth animation, then asks players to guide hero Dirk the Daring through precisely timed joystick and button choices.

Rick Dyer's Advanced Microcomputer Systems developed the game with Don Bluth Studios and Cinematronics. Its branching scenes offer only limited control compared with conventional action games, but the spectacle is immediate: a coin-operated cartoon whose hero lives or dies on the player's cue.

The attraction also exposes the technology's tradeoffs. Memorization matters, wrong moves end quickly, and laserdisc hardware is more elaborate than ordinary game boards. Even so, Dragon's Lair is the summer's clearest sign that Hollywood craft and arcade machinery are converging.

stories.headline: Atari Clears the Deck for XL
stories.dek: The 400, 800, and 1200XL give way to a new family led by the $199 600XL and $299 800XL.
body: Atari is replacing its established computer line in one sweep. The company has discontinued the 400, 800, and recently introduced 1200XL in favor of four XL models, a drastic reset during the fiercest home-computer price competition yet.

The 16K 600XL is listed at $199 and can expand to 64K; the 64K 800XL is $299. Both build BASIC into ROM, retain compatibility with most earlier Atari software and peripherals, and expose a full processor bus for expansion.

Atari is also looking beyond its own hardware. A new publishing arm plans software for Commodore and Texas Instruments computers, acknowledging that popular programs may have to travel wherever the customers are.
